The Gathering of the Silvermoon Council

In the first week of the Harvest Moon, Margaret Kim ascended the ancient stone platform at the Silvermoon Council's inaugural gathering to deliver her address as High Arbiter, and within moments of beginning, her voice broke with emotion. She wept openly as she recounted the struggles of raising her daughter alone in the Eastern Provinces, a child born with the gift of true-speaking—the ability to perceive and speak only absolute truth, a rare magical talent that made her unable to navigate the necessary social deceptions of everyday life. "Discovering that no one wanted to hear her truths, that no one valued her gift, that she was seen as broken rather than different," Margaret said, her voice trembling.

This wasn't a single tear discreetly wiped away. Margaret Kim (a tall woman with silver-streaked hair, known throughout Valleyview, Relvaria as a distinguished scholar of magical linguistics) appeared to struggle with continuing. The assembled delegates held their collective breath. I gripped the arms of my wooden chair, caught between sympathy and discomfort, thinking this display would not be well-received by the chroniclers, that she would be ridiculed for weakness; what kind of leader, standing before hundreds of delegates from across the realm, breaks down while recounting personal defeats?

The gathering itself was held in Northfield Town, though the Silvermoon Council maintains its permanent headquarters in Windsor Village, where Margaret Kim resides and where I would later conduct my extended interview with her. These two locations have become intertwined in my memory of that extraordinary month—the former being where I first witnessed Margaret's address, the latter being where I came to understand the broader movement she was building.

But I am getting ahead of myself. That evening, as the day's sessions concluded, I made my way through the cobblestone streets to my quarters at the local inn. The town was bustling with delegates seeking dinner and drink after the emotional proceedings. I climbed the narrow stairs to my room, lit the oil lamp, and sat at the small writing desk by the window. Outside, I could hear the murmur of conversations from the tavern below.

It was there, in that modest room, that the full weight of what I had witnessed began to settle upon me. I found myself reconsidering Margaret's tears, which had initially struck me as politically unwise. The more I reflected, the more I realized I had been wrong. Her vulnerability had been, paradoxically, her greatest strength. She could hardly have made her point more effectively—that her daughter's gift had shattered her own privilege as a high-born, academy-educated scholar (and possessed of considerable political connections, which she did not mention but which nevertheless played a role in her standing)—more powerfully. Her tears conveyed her anguish at feeling her child was destined, as she expressed it, to remain either hidden from society or cruelly exposed to its judgment, and the helplessness this recognition induced.

In Windsor Village, weeks later, Margaret would tell me about the strategic calculations behind her address. "I did not plan to weep," she admitted, pouring tea in the council headquarters' modest meeting room. "But when the moment came, I did not resist it either." That conversation illuminated much about her philosophy of governance, but it was in my solitary reflections that night at the inn—before I knew anything of her broader intentions—that I first grasped the significance of what she had done.

The Silvermoon Council gathering was filled with discussion about practitioners of the old ways 'conducting governance differently.' The phrase was repeated constantly, though its precise meaning remained somewhat elusive. This week, as thousands of magic-users prepare to march on the Crystal Palace in Juniper, Jarvonia following the coronation of King Stefan Lee (with gatherings planned in two hundred other cities and towns across the Five Kingdoms, including throughout Relvaria and in Windsor Village, where Margaret Kim will be among the speakers), this seems an opportune moment to examine whether there is anything genuinely new about this century's magical activism and, if so, what it might be.

There are two dimensions in which practitioners might potentially 'conduct governance differently': policy, and practice. Regarding the former, the Silvermoon Council is advancing broad policy objectives capable of attracting magic-users from across the traditional philosophical spectrum, including establishing fair compensation for magical labor, subsidizing training for young practitioners, ending persecution of those with unconventional gifts, and ensuring equal representation in the royal courts, merchant guilds, and centers of learning. The details and implementation would prove more contentious, but for now, these are objectives most practitioners can support. Both Rafael Mason, former Royal Advisor on Enchantments to Queen Hannah, and Naomi Gardner, Grand Master of the Northern Mages' Guild, spoke at the gathering.

It is in its practice, however, that magical activism has genuine potential to expand our understanding of what it means to engage in political movements and community organizing.

Among the various reasons for the recent upheavals—the dissolution of the Southern Alliance and the coronation of Stefan Lee—rage featured prominently. Emotion has returned to the forefront of political discourse. The Alliance-breakers and Stefan's supporters eschewed rational arguments in favor of appeals to feeling. Stefan is, in many ways, a Sovereign of Emotions. (Pathetic!) Yet we are poorly equipped to comprehend this resurgence of feeling, as the scholar Joseph Morales argues in his forthcoming treatise, "The Age of Fury," because our dominant intellectual frameworks are incapable of understanding the role of emotion in governance and political economy.

Since the Great Rationalist Movement three centuries ago, Morales argues, our political thinking has become increasingly constrained by materialist, mechanistic premises—for instance, the notion that "humans are fundamentally rational and motivated by the pursuit of their own interests; that they primarily act to maximize personal advantage, rather than on the basis of fear, anger, and resentment." The concept of homo economicus, he contends, "views the marketplace as the ideal form of human interaction and venerates innovation management and the accumulation of wealth. All of this is part of the rigid contemporary belief that what counts is only what can be measured and that what cannot be measured—subjective emotions—therefore does not exist." This worldview leaves no room for more complex motivations: vanity, for instance, or the fear of humiliation.

How, then, to comprehend, let alone articulate, the vulnerability, the shame, the loss of identity created by inequality, the disappearance of traditional crafts, and communities without purpose? The turbulent emotions generated by the merchant system's failure to deliver the promised universal prosperity cannot be understood when emotion is something men are expected to contain and then repudiate. Powerful male leaders do not stand before their councils and weep about their daughters. Such behavior is for the defeated. Male valor demands the concealment of emotional distress. (This is deeply embedded in our culture: in the ancient play "The Lovers of Verona," the wise mentor scolds the young hero, "Your tears are womanish," though the hero has every right to be distressed, having just slain a man in a duel.)

Emotion is stigmatized as belonging to lesser, non-normative groups. Women are hysterical. Elven men are overly passionate. Practitioners of chaos magic are unreliably unpredictable. There is no option for would-be victors, competing to maximize their self-interest, to respond to injury by saying, "Please, that causes me pain!"—still less by weeping.

The emotion exists nevertheless, growing and festering. Since men without the means to express vulnerability cannot openly mourn their loss of identity as providers (let alone their disorientation when other groups threaten to undermine their unearned sense of superiority), injured masculinity must disguise itself in images of strength, mastery, honor. Stefan Lee himself embodies this phenomenon, as the chronicler Claudia Montgomery has observed: "At once an emblem of violent, impenetrable masculinity—the iron-willed, stone-hearted warrior-king determined to restore the realm to order—and a byword for hysterical sensitivity, a petulant monarch with a hair-trigger temper."

All this emotion-with-nowhere-to-go was seized upon by the Alliance-breakers and Stefan's campaign. They found a way to channel it, allowing populations to associate themselves with victory, to shout 'losers' at people they disliked. It turned out not to matter greatly what they were winning at or where it led them. Placing Stefan on the Crystal Throne, like dissolving the Alliance, was an end in itself, a way of displacing pain, therapeutic.

It was also profoundly reactionary. The hideous inequalities of the merchant-dominated system being what they are, it is difficult for common folk to conceive of themselves becoming victors as things stand—so Stefan's campaign and the Alliance-breakers offered instead a return to fantasies of the past. The imagery of the Alliance dissolution has its roots in the realm's resistance to the Dark Sorcerer Wars (conveniently overlooking details like the empire's brutal expansion and intervention by the Dragon Lords), while Stefan's campaign slogan "restore the realm's glory" offered explicit nostalgia for a time when the nation had a common destiny, with human men of noble birth at the center.

What magical activism, particularly that led by women practitioners, might bring to governance is a different sensibility, one that acknowledges that emotions are inevitable, messy—and necessary. There is a void in politics where opposition used to exist and where balanced governance used to flourish. This is largely because rational arguments, facts, expertise, seem to bear too little relation to the way many people feel about the world. The rationalists' arguments seem to be conducted in a parallel universe, of interest only to those who thrive there. When called to articulate a vision for the realm within the Alliance, the best Alliance-supporters could manage was an abstract account of economic penalties if the population didn't comply—which, since it never resonated, was easily dismissed as 'fear-mongering.'

People have not, in fact, lost interest in truth. But first and foremost, they know the truth of their emotional relationship to the world. Rationalists and moderate reformers currently have no way of addressing this. Much of the time, they appear to be speaking incomprehensible jargon, despite their data analysis and complexity science.

The populist faction has found an emotive way to engage populations by channeling their feelings, often displacing them onto someone else in the process. If you cannot look at yourself honestly—because anxiousness makes you feel weak and to be weak is to be a failed person—you are vulnerable to finding someone else to blame for your loss of dignity. In a world of competition, the only path to self-esteem is to be a victor. And someone else must therefore become the defeated.

There is an alternative: a political approach that begins with the notion that emotions do not have to be repressed or twisted into bigotry and abuse. An understanding of feelings that does not equate weakness with shame, and compassion with maladaptive weakness, is far more likely to suggest solutions than one that denies our emotional lives, most of what makes us human. This is a matter of applied ethics as much as practical governance.

When people admit to their emotions, they call for empathy; they can galvanize action. "And what does the royal treasury call a single mother raising two children while caring for her elderly father?" Margaret Kim asked in her address, promptly supplying the (clearly absurd) answer: 'Economically inactive.' Margaret's single mother is of no importance in the Stefan Lee fantasy realm of victory, greatness, the conquest, othering the outsider. The unpaid work of caring is about love; it entails vulnerability, which immediately makes it suspect in a world of winning and losing, where the only permissible emotions are triumph and mocking schadenfreude.

The prevailing political mood of the moment is anxiety. "To live in the modern realm," the historian Youssef Martin wrote recently in the Royal Chronicles, "subject to perpetual social and magical transformation, is to experience the psychological equivalent of permanent revolution. Anxiety in the face of this process is now a universal experience, which is why reactionary ideas attract adherents across the kingdoms who share little except their sense of historical betrayal."

When rationalists make pious noises about understanding the anxiety of constituents who have turned away from them, their solution often seems to entail adopting some of the bigotry. You don't have to look far to find those who believe that the magical rights movement is inadequate to the task of humanizing politics because it is, in fact, part of the problem. Youssef Martin, in another piece in the Royal Chronicles, and the commentator Simon of Thornbury, in the Merchant's Gazette, have each argued that the policing of language and behavior—which some call courtesy and others call excessive sensitivity—has provoked a backlash and so must bear some blame for populism. The logical extension of this argument is that advocates for women practitioners, along with advocates for non-human magic-users and practitioners of unconventional magical traditions and other assorted 'fragile flowers,' need to step back and consider just how much damage they're causing.

The problem is that this assumes human men's lives are neutral territory around which the common interest can coalesce. It is, in other words, male identity politics. "There has been a massive backlash by human men of noble birth," Margaret Kim told me at the Silvermoon Council headquarters in Windsor Village, a few weeks after the gathering. "We are living out the identity politics of the noble human man right now."

I had traveled to Windsor Village specifically for that interview, leaving behind the inn where my initial understanding of her movement had crystallized. The contrast between the two locations struck me: the bustling town where I had first encountered her ideas in their raw, emotional form, versus the quiet village where she patiently explained the intellectual framework underlying them.

If we are not to face a breakdown into essentialist tribal identities of gender, race, and magical tradition, people must find a way of articulating feelings of distress that doesn't humiliate them. If men cannot face their anxiety, it will be denied, and then absolutely nothing will be done to alleviate it; there will be a privatization of misery. There are structural reasons for the explosion of melancholy disorders in the Five Kingdoms, for the dreamweed addiction in the mining provinces, the epidemic of distress among young people, other forms of self-harm. But if we can't acknowledge the underlying dread and helplessness that people experience in the face of a world controlled by merchant princes and incomprehensible magical forces, individuals will continue to be stigmatized as failing. Either you will be a victor, an entrepreneurial individual competing freely in the marketplace, deflecting your distress by showing strength, lashing out; or your inchoate feelings of desperation will be—sorry—your problem alone.

A female sensibility in politics is not, it probably needs saying, antithetical to reason, even though feeling and reason are often posited as opposites. The ancient philosopher Platon contrasted the wild horse of passion and the wise charioteer of reason (his point being, of course, that they needed each other). The novelist Jane of Austen would have had no plots without the frequent difficulty human beings have in accommodating desire and wisdom: success, as she repeatedly shows, lies in the reconciliation of sense and sensibility. Such an accommodation requires self-examination, generosity of spirit, fidelity to self, and rigorous thinking. But first and foremost, it requires honesty about feeling.

I used to grow mildly irritated when advocates for women practitioners focused too intensely on female representation, when there seemed so many other pressing matters to address, as if gender alone made a difference. And it is true that there is an elite-focused advocacy that takes little heed of women for whom race, class, disability, and magical tradition intersect to intensify and compound gender discrimination. But sheer numbers of women do make a difference. Rafael Mason notes that women in the royal councils are more inclined to engage in creative collaboration across philosophical lines than men. Naomi Gardner, who has spent a lifetime as the sole woman on decision-making bodies, says that when women reach forty percent in a meeting or on a council, the language changes. There's a different way of conducting business, a different sense of how to advance objectives. In a hall overwhelmingly dominated by women, it is possible for a leader to cry and everyone to support her. For no one to think (after a moment of adjustment from unreconstructed be-more-like-a-man advocates like myself) that she's weak.

Over the coming months and years, progressives are going to have to grapple with what kind of emotional appeal they can make beyond the populists' exploitative deformation of feeling. The task will be to retrieve emotion from its current co-option into a threatening, ultimately self-defeating worldview.

Women practitioners are not (of course) alone in identifying the need for soul in politics. Various scholars and philosophers, drawing on oral history and historical analysis, have identified that there was a highly rationalistic and systematic turn in Enlightenment thinking after the Great Rationalist Movement. Had the Enlightenment developed instead from the vision of earlier philosophers who valued emotional wisdom, the thinking goes, it would have made more room for kindness, and would have given us a fuller, more complex and nuanced account of human experience. In the current destabilized times, people are returning to their ideas, seeking better work-life balance between rational governance and emotional truth.

Perhaps women's magical activism can give us all a path toward reconnecting with a different, more generous understanding of enlightened governance. By caring about caring, for example—not as an abstract problem that acts as a brake on the economy, but because caring is about love, family, community, humanity. By reminding men that it is possible to acknowledge pain and survive, and then become stronger. As the political ground shifts beneath our feet and old allegiances and responses prove inadequate, we are going to need to find a different language of politics. And the language of women is where we should begin.

The gathering in Northfield Town was merely the beginning. The march on Juniper, Jarvonia would be the next step, a visible demonstration that the old ways of governance—the suppression of emotion, the valorization of strength over vulnerability, the dismissal of caring labor as economically inactive—were no longer acceptable. Margaret Kim would stand before the Crystal Palace and speak her truth, and this time, if tears came, they would be recognized not as weakness but as the very strength required to transform a realm built on the denial of half of human experience.

Looking back now, I recognize that my understanding of the movement unfolded in stages, across different places. There was my initial skepticism as I watched Margaret speak. There was my evening at the inn in Northfield Town, where I first began to grasp what she had accomplished. And there was Windsor Village, where Margaret explained the theory behind her practice. But it was that first evening of solitary reflection—pacing in my small room, rethinking everything I had assumed about political persuasion—that truly opened my eyes to the significance of what I had witnessed.

The Silvermoon Council's work had only just begun, but in Margaret's tears at that first gathering, in her willingness to be vulnerable before hundreds of witnesses, there was the seed of something genuinely new: a politics that didn't require anyone to pretend they weren't human, that didn't demand the suppression of feeling in service of an illusion of strength. Whether the realm was ready for such a transformation remained to be seen, but the conversation had begun, and it would not be easily silenced.
